extracted.intended_audience: scientists, legal scholars/judges, and educated readers concerned with principles of evidence and testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for assessing human testimony and claims in science and courts, including who counts as an expert, how to classify claims by evidentiary requirement, and what practices are unscientific. Applies to investigating, admitting, and weighing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method as guide to principles of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The reform of logic and principles of evidence should advance under the guidance of the scientific method — defined as the method of obtaining and organizing knowledge which consists in defining, so far as possible to expert human faculties, the boundaries between the possible and the probable, between the known and the unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undertake evaluation in a scientific (constructive, not skeptical) spirit: aim to reconstruct human testimony by clarifying what is possible/probable/known/unknown. Use the intellect alone, minimize emotional influence, and define limits of knowledge when judging claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific sense (mental attitude required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific sense is the power of seeking truth through the intellect alone, uninfluenced by the emotions; it has no hopes and no fears except as they may help to find the truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should cultivate dispassionate, truth-seeking attitudes and avoid letting emotions, wishful thinking, or fears influence assessment of testimony and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cornerstone: rely on expert testimony for scientific matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The recognition of the necessity of the testimony only of experts in all matters of science, and consequent absolute rejection of all testimony of non-experts, without reference to their number or the unanimity of their testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims that pertain to scientific questions, non-expert testimony—even if numerous or unanimous—should be treated as scientifically inadmissible; rely on appropriately qualified experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: science, expert, non-expert
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is systematized knowledge. An expert is one who can see all sides of a subject. A non-expert is one who sees but one or a few sides of a subject that has many sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these working definitions when deciding who may legitimately assess or testify about a claim; identify whether a claimant/witness is an expert (broad perspective) or a non-expert (limited view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests of scientific expertness
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests include: distrust of the senses; recognition of the relation of induction to deduction; avoidance of all sources of error in observation, experiment, or reasoning; appreciation of the relative importance and non-importance of real or supposed facts; ability to distinguish reality and its semblance (especially subjective vs objective); maintenance of mental equilibrium during experimental researches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess potential experts by these behavioral/intellectual signs. Reputation is acquired primarily through other experts; expertness has degrees (originators vs followers). Examples: Newton or Galileo as highest experts who may stand alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests of scientific non-expertness (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of non-expertness include: blind repose in the senses; inability to eliminate or appreciate sources of error in observation, experiment, or reasoning; non-appreciation of relative importance of facts; confounding semblance with reality, particularly subjective with objective; liability to be entranced or have emotions unduly excited; misuse of induction/deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat testimony or analysis showing these traits as unreliable. Be wary of witnesses or commentators who rely on senses uncritically, who confuse appearance for reality, or who let emotion drive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specificity and limits of expertness
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness in one branch of science not only does not qualify, but in various ways may disqualify, one to be an expert in another branch; eminence in one specialty may unfit one for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize an individual's authority across specialties; when referring a claim, choose experts from the specialty best suited to the question. Recognize that highest experts sometimes create new standards and may initially stand alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation and referral to appropriate specialty
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should primarily be referred to that specialty that is best capable of dealing with it by deductive reasoning. If the claim can be settled by principles of logic, refer to logicians. The primary expert judges whether cooperation of experts in other branches is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a complex claim, first identify the primary specialty; seek cooperation only as judged necessary by that primary expert. If a domain is not yet organized into a science (no experts), then no authoritative decision can be made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and quantity of evidence depend on nature of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality and quantity of evidence necessary for proof of any claim depends on the nature of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply different evidentiary standards to different classes of claims rather than a one-size-fits-all rule; more extraordinary or novel claims require higher quality and quantity of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class I claims: everyday/unsystematized knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as to unsystematized knowledge or matters of every-day life: for these claims experts are not usually required, and mistakes are of comparatively trifling account since they affect individuals and not general principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary testimony admitted in courts of justice often falls here. From a scientific standpoint, some legal evidence rules (e.g., exclusion of hearsay) may be unscientific; for many practical purposes non-expert testimony is tolerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class II claims: facts of science already established by experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as to general or special facts of science that are already established by the investigations of experts: here we rise in scale of evidence, but do not require experts; what is bad or useless evidence for original demonstration may be satisfactory for confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept non-expert statements as confirmation when the underlying scientific fact is established (e.g., after the phonograph was invented, non-experts could credibly report on it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class III claims: not yet established but possibly provable by future experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as to facts or phenomena which have not yet been established by experts but which may yet be proved true by the experts of the future: these cannot be proved by any amount of non-expert evidence; non-expert testimony may only arouse experts to investigate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept non-expert testimony as proof for novel scientific claims (e.g., sea-serpent, proposed new forces). Use such testimony only as a prompt for expert investigation; ultimate judgment belongs to experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class IV claims: inherently unprovable or supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims which, from the limitations of the human faculties, can never be proved or disproved (e.g., supernatural claims): they may be indulged in as speculations, but to seriously discuss them with purpose of ascertaining truth or falsity is unscientific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat supernatural assertions as outside the scope of scientific proof; attempting scientific demonstration of religion or supernatural phenomena is category error and unproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class V claims: absolutely disproved by deductive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims which are absolutely disproved by deductive reasoning, and which therefore the special sciences to which they belong know to be false without any examination (examples: squaring the circle, flatness of the earth, perpetual motion, alchemy, astrology, levitation, mind-reading, clairvoyance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is unscientific and useless to examine or discuss such claims for the purpose of determining their truth; they should be rejected a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal trials as experiments with living human beings — guard against six sources of error
rubrics_metrics.description: From the scientific point of view, a legal trial is really an experiment with living human beings and, like all experiments of that kind, is liable to six sources of error, all of which must be guarded against to find the exact truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that court procedures often impair or destroy the scientific value of testimony; when using trial testimony as evidence, account for experimental error sources (emotional effects, suggestion, etc.) and design safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision of expert conclusions by other/better experts
rubrics_metrics.description: When experts blunder their conclusions should be revised, not by the people, but by other and better experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid popular or non-expert challenges to expert conclusions; corrections should come through expert critique and improved expertise within the scientific community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three unpardonable scientific sins to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: In science there are three unpardonable sins — trusting the senses, non-experts attempting to do the work of experts, and using deduction for induction or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reliance on raw senses, amateur intrusion into expert domains, and misuse of reasoning modes as fundamental methodological errors that invalidate inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative order for new claims: known → unknown → supernatural
rubrics_metrics.description: In investigating new claims, experts first inquire whether the claims can be explained by laws already known; if not, they refer the claim to the unknown in Nature and attempt to bring it into the known; asserting supernatural character abandons scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this diagnostic order when assessing novel phenomena. Reserve supernatural explanations only when all possibilities within nature have been exhaustively considered — but recognize that such a differential diagnosis between unknown and supernatural is effectively impossible.
